en: The Sūtra on the Four Classes Spoken by the Buddha, translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Zhu Fahu of the Yuezhi Kingdom during the Western Jin Dynasty.
Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park. At that time...

At that time, the fourfold assembly of disciples, the celestial emperors, nāgas, ghosts, spirits, and kumbhāṇḍas, all proceeded to the Jeta Grove, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and withdrew to sit in their respective places.
The Buddha addressed his disciples:
"All the sutras and teachings I have now brought forth, and all my instructions, must each be preserved within your own minds.

In the future age, when it is filled with poison, the disciples of the fourfold assembly—whether they be monastics or householders practicing the Way—will become intoxicated by the manifold sensory objects and no longer accept or apply the Buddha’s sutras and teachings. Being exclusively foolish and self-opinionated, they will cause my Way to become thin and flavorless, leading worldly people to slander my Way; believe that this is caused by the arrogance of these disciples!"
Śāriputra adjusted his robes, joined his palms, and listened with single-minded devotion as the Buddha preached the *Catuṣpariṣat-sūtra* in this manner.
The Buddha said:

"If, in the final age, a man is able to leave the household life and shave his hair for the sake of the Way, he must first distance himself from craving and desire, set his resolve upon the Mahāyāna, and always take loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity as his primary guides. He should eliminate [unwholesome] thoughts and actions, universally mind all classes of living beings—whether flying or crawling—and regard them as no different from his own body, never allowing anger or resentment to arise."

Deeply entering the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*), one constantly employs the skillful means (*upāya*) of the perfection of wisdom to guide those who are ignorant and deluded, causing them to enter the infinite. Through the virtue of the precepts, one eliminates the diseases of mental defilement and must not engage in worldly activities.
Those who can practice this may leave the household life and be called "Path-makers" (daoshi).
One must not rely upon my Dharma alone, taking the mere act of leaving home as proof of faith while failing to focus single-mindedly on the Path.
There may be those of lowly status who rely on the Way for their livelihood, yet provide no benefit to anyone and merely speak out of their own whims.

Acting as teachers and leaders, they are frivolous and mocking, failing to exercise self-restraint, thereby causing the honored Dharma to become thin and diluted. That people of the world do not believe them is not the way of my disciples who have left the household life!
The Buddha said:

"If there are women who leave the household life, shave their heads to pursue the Way, and seek to eliminate craving and desire, they must apply themselves with single-minded diligence in a quiet place and must not reside in the same temple as ordained men."
If one practices the transmission of the teachings, there must be companions of equal standing; one must not go alone to receive instruction.
One should always leave late and return early, and must not go out recklessly to stay overnight at a temple.
One may instruct women, but one must not instruct men.
As for the garments one wears, they must not be embroidered with silk, nor dyed with colorful pigments, nor scented with fragrances.
One must not speak frivolously or engage in jesting, nor covet wealth or precious objects; one whose conduct is pure in this way is called a renunciant practitioner.

If one speaks frivolously and playfully, laughs prematurely before others have spoken, lacks tranquility of mind and will, acts with defiled intentions, uses harsh speech and insults, is unrestrained in idle talk, cannot remain in stillness, is arrogant and conceited, and fails to exercise self-restraint—even though such a person has left the household life, they are still a base individual and not a disciple of the renunciant path!
The Buddha said:

"If there is a man whose mind and will are set upon the Path, yet he is unable to leave the household life, he should, while remaining amidst desires and attachments, uphold the five precepts and observe the six fast days each month."
First, be filial and obedient to one's parents, managing the household and raising one's children;
burn incense and light lamps morning and evening, prostrate before the Triple Gem, repent before the ten directions, and show reverence to the fourfold assembly;
do not be arrogant, conceited, or disdainful, and abandon stinginess and greed.
One must always act with utmost sincerity and must not deceive or exploit worldly people;
one must not sit or rise on the same mat as the wives of worldly people, nor accompany them in walking or staying, nor share a room with them even if on separate beds.
Setting aside these four matters, one regards all beings universally with the four immeasurable minds: those who are old are regarded as fathers or mothers;
those who are young are regarded as younger brothers or sons.
One should constantly use the medicinal elixir of the *prajñāpāramitā* to wash away the various ailments of sentient beings; one must not give way to groundless anger or revile others.
One should always employ infinite skillful means (*upāya*) to guide and liberate worldly people, leading them into the Mahāyāna;

one must not preach profound sutras or the most subtle and wondrous meanings to those who are newly initiated learners, but should instead teach those who have eliminated conceptualizations and consciousness, and are free from all obstructions.
One must not adorn one’s robes with finery, nor engage in playful conversation or exchange greetings with worldly wives and daughters;
by avoiding such causes and conditions, one becomes a pure practitioner of the Way.
If one's conduct is impure, craving wealth, profit, and sensual beauty;
or if, regarding the finery and ornaments of the secular world, they vie with one another for display, forming bonds that are not evil yet fixated on desire;
or if they speak lightly and flirtatiously, laughing prematurely before even a word has been spoken.
They rely on themselves as fellow practitioners of the Dharma and speak wondrous words with their mouths;
outwardly they appear pure and detached, yet inwardly they harbor greed and delusion;
their minds are fixed on wealth and goods to provide for themselves and to sustain their wives and children.

They show arrogance toward the Buddha and the honored scriptures, no longer practicing or studying them; instead, they practice the arts of external paths—worldly medical prescriptions and petitions, talismans, incantations, and exorcisms, as well as the causal methods for treating various diseases and the arts of petitioning used by external paths. Or, they manipulate wealth and property between superiors and subordinates, harboring thieving intentions to acquire gain through these arts of petitioning. Because they do not uphold my Dharma, those who will come in the future shall all be of this ilk; therefore, they are not disciples who study my Dharma!
The Buddha said:
"If there are women who cannot leave the household life, yet within their hearts of desire and passion delight in the Way, they should uphold the five precepts and observe the six monthly fasts."
One must be filial and obedient toward one's parents, sisters-in-law, elder and younger brothers, and sisters;
one must not beat or scold one's children or female servants;
and one must not travel lightly to stay overnight at the homes of others.
One must not engage in speech with worldly men that is flirtatious or mocking;
one must not give way to groundless anger, revile others, or use harsh speech;
one must not testify to the faults of others, nor entrap others by exposing the transgressions of their children, wives, concubines, or slaves.
One should always be single-mindedly diligent in mindfulness of the Way as one's primary focus;
one must not preach the Dharma with a worldly or ordinary countenance;
one must not engage in mutual disparagement with men, nor should one instruct other men.
One must not speak of worldly omens of fortune or misfortune, of good or evil, or of signs of calamity;
one must not be arrogant or conceited;

three times each day and night, one should burn incense, prostrate before the Triple Gem, repent before the ten directions, receive and practice the sutras, and constantly exhort oneself through verbal recitation.
One must not hope for offerings, nor covet profit or wealth;

one must not harbor jealousy toward her husband, but should instead despise the female body, vowing to become a man in a future life to receive blessings and attain rebirth in the celestial palaces of the heavens where things appear spontaneously.
This is the Dharma for a laywoman of pure faith who studies the Way.

If she is not filial and obedient, is arrogant toward her parents-in-law, is jealous of her husband, beats and reviles her servants, commits evil while considering herself right, and harbors resentment, anger, and poisonous intent toward others—if a practitioner acts in such a way, she is a disciple of women who studies in a manner contrary to the Dharma!
The Buddha addressed his disciples:

"Purify and guard your minds; protect your bodies and speech. Constantly deliver all sentient beings through the four immeasurables, and bestow the wisdom of the jewel of the Path upon all. Following the Buddha’s instructions, you shall surely attain liberation from the world!"

The disciples and all those gathered in the assembly, having heard the Buddha preach this sutra, rejoiced and practiced it accordingly; they prostrated and departed. Thus concludes the *Sutra on the Four Classes of Disciples* preached by the Buddha.
